paras: The killing of Robert E. Banks was the fatal shooting of an 18-year-old youth by a gang of white boys and men on Josephine street near Howard in New Orleans on the evening of November 6, 1903. Three white boys were arrested, and a white man, Gus Drew, later surrendered saying he had fired in self defense. The case is known from a New Orleans correspondent's letter to the Richmond Planet, which called it an "unprovoked murder."

Between 8 and 9 o'clock that Friday evening, Banks was returning from a drug store with medicine for his ill sister. A gang of boys and men met him and began throwing stones, and as he ran one of them cried out to kill him and not let him get away. Two shots followed; according to the correspondent, Banks was unarmed and was hit in the back while running. He fell, got up, walked one block to his sister's home, and died within ten minutes from a bullet that had passed through his left lung.

Three white boys were arrested, and their trial was set for Tuesday, November 24. Before then Gus Drew came into the custody of officers, saying that he had killed Banks and had done so in self defense. The correspondent called the claim "ridiculous" and implied that Drew came forward to shield the three arrested. No report of the trial's outcome was found.

The Richmond Planet printed the letter, dated November 22, on its front page of November 28 under the headlines "A Brutal Murder" and "An Unprovoked Murder." The writer tied the case to Richmond readers through Banks's brother-in-law, R. E. Dandridge, whose brother lived in that city. He called the attackers "white hoodlums," vouched for Banks as a "model youth" of an excellent family, and predicted that the trial would end unjustly.

His defense of Banks's character answered the New Orleans Daily News, which, he wrote, had described the youth as "A Nigger Bully." No white-press report of the shooting or trial appears in the coverage; the Daily News's account survives only in this quotation.

The only report is one Black correspondent's letter in the Richmond Planet, printed in two segments (A1, A2); no white-press or other Black-press account was found, and Drew's self-defense claim is known only second-hand through that letter.
